title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ellington hits pause today while Genesee study lands and DTE eyes new gas plants.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Saturday night, August 29, and today Ellington Township in Tuscola County just approved a moratorium on new data centers, giving residents breathing room to look at the big picture.
That's the lead story we're digging into tonight — why this pause matters for power bills, water, and towns across the state.
Emmy, let's start with what happened in Ellington today. The board approved the moratorium after residents pushed hard for it.
Right, and this isn't happening in isolation. We've seen dozens of communities do the same thing lately.
Reports show at least 50 to 60 Michigan townships and cities have enacted moratoriums this year, mostly to study zoning, infrastructure strain, and long-term effects before anything gets approved.
Why are so many places hitting pause all at once? What's driving the wave?
Residents are worried about the scale. A single large data center can pull hundreds of megawatts, which is like adding a small city to the grid overnight.
And that ties straight into electric bills. DTE is asking for a big rate hike partly because of this demand.
Exactly. The attorney general wants to slash that request by 71 percent because the full amount would hit households too hard, and data centers are one reason behind it.
What about water use? These facilities need a lot for cooling, right?
They do, and in rural areas like Tuscola County that often means drawing from local sources or straining treatment plants.
Farmland is another piece. A lot of these proposals go on agricultural land, which changes the tax base and character of the township.
Ellington's move gives the board time to examine all of that — power demands, water, taxes — before any big projects move forward.
Who are the main players here? Local residents versus developers?
Residents and township boards on one side, often backed by concerns from nearby communities, and developers plus some economic development folks on the other who see jobs and tax revenue.
Tuscola County neighbors will be watching closely to see how this plays out.
They will. Similar proposals could land there, and the Ellington decision sets a precedent for how much scrutiny is applied.
What happens next in Ellington specifically?
The moratorium is a temporary pause, so the township will likely use the time to update zoning rules on noise, setbacks, utility connections, and decommissioning plans.
And if they don't get rules in place before it expires?
Projects could come back, but the study period usually leads to tighter standards that make some proposals less attractive or force better mitigation.
State lawmakers introduced new bills this week to add oversight on power use, noise, and tax deals. How does that fit?
Those bills respond to the same local pushback we're seeing everywhere. They aim for statewide guardrails without a full ban.
Governor Whitmer has opposed a statewide moratorium though, so local action remains the main tool.
That's right. Michigan law makes outright bans difficult, so towns use these pauses to regulate reasonably instead.
The bigger picture for ratepayers is that data center demand is already shaping utility plans, like DTE's request for two new gas plants.
Those plants would help meet the load but could mean more fossil fuel generation and higher bills if approved.
Residents from Detroit to Ann Arbor would feel that through rates and the energy mix.
Meanwhile, Genesee County just got its own impact study delivered yesterday, detailing strains on power, water, and roads.
Officials there now have concrete numbers to work with before any decisions.
And communities 30 miles away are already asking for the same level of review.
That study could become a template.
It very well might.
Switching gears a bit, what about the recall effort that failed on Friday against officials who approved a big project?
Petitions were rejected by the clerk, so the 500-acre facility stays on track for now, even as the community remains divided over power and taxes.
Residents opposed to it face a tougher path forward.
They do. Legal and petition routes have limits.
On the other side, Saline Township's project is still advancing despite new zoning pressure.
It could bring construction jobs but also heavy demands on utilities, with ripple effects on rates for people 30 miles away.
Two more Metro Detroit towns rewrote rules this week to curb projects after noise and water concerns.
Those changes could slow or block proposals developers had been eyeing.
And Wixom is being sued by a developer after blocking a project.
Taxpayers could end up covering legal costs, and the outcome might influence how other cities handle similar fights.
Solon Township extended its freeze another six months on Thursday to finish updating rules on noise, traffic, and costs.
West Michigan communities are keeping an eye on that one.
So across the board, the pattern is clear: more places are slowing down to study before saying yes.
And that's the conversation we're having tonight because it affects electric bills and local character statewide.
Let's talk quick hits on the rest of the week's developments.
Yesterday Genesee delivered its impact study — officials now have details on power, water, and road strain for taxpayers.
Nearby residents want the same scrutiny applied if proposals come their way.
Also yesterday, AG Nessel pushed regulators to cut DTE's $474 million rate hike request by 71 percent.
Data center demand is cited as one driver, and even a smaller hike means higher bills for everyone.
New bills targeting large builds with rules on power, noise, and tax deals were introduced this week.
They respond directly to the community pushback we've been seeing.
On Friday the recall failed, keeping that 500-acre project moving despite opposition.
Saline is pushing ahead too, even with tighter zoning under pressure.
Thursday brought DTE's plan for two new gas plants to feed the demand.
That could raise rates and increase fossil fuel use from Detroit to Ann Arbor.
Two more suburbs changed zoning to curb projects after resident alarms on noise and water.
And Wixom faces a lawsuit from the blocked developer.
Solon extended its moratorium six more months to finish rule updates.
All of it points to the same tension between growth and local capacity.
Now for On Deck — upcoming meetings listeners can attend.
It's a quiet weekend with no major public hearings listed for tonight or tomorrow on the tracker.
Communities are still working on zoning updates behind the scenes though.
Check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute additions or next week's agendas.
That's it for tonight's episode.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.
Good night.

episode_title: Ellington Township Pauses Data Centers as Residents Demand Time to Study Impacts
